questions.stem: A nurse sustains a hollow-bore needlestick from a patient whose HIV status is not immediately available. After washing the site, which action is the priority?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Wait for the source patient's final laboratory result before reporting the exposure because treatment decisions should not begin until infection is confirmed.","B":"Monitor for fever or rash for several days and seek care only if symptoms appear because post-exposure treatment is unnecessary before symptoms develop.","C":"Schedule routine employee-health testing for the following week because occupational HIV exposure is not considered time-sensitive when source status is unknown.","D":"Report the exposure and obtain urgent medical evaluation for PEP; when indicated, treatment should start as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours."}}
questions.rationale: CDC treats potential HIV exposure as time-sensitive. Occupational exposures should be reported and medically evaluated immediately. When PEP is indicated, it should be started as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after exposure; source testing should not create unnecessary delay in evaluation.
questions.source_name: CDC — Preventing HIV with PEP: Workplace Exposures
questions.source_detail: Current CDC PEP page, workplace-exposure section: report occupational exposure and seek medical attention immediately; PEP must start within 72 hours and sooner is better. Reviewed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: An uninsured client with an unpaid prior hospital balance presents to a Medicare-participating emergency department with symptoms suggesting an emergency medical condition. What does EMTALA require?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The hospital must provide an appropriate medical screening examination and, if an emergency condition exists, offer stabilizing treatment regardless of payment.","B":"The hospital may obtain payment information before the screening examination whenever triage suggests the client is stable enough to wait for financial counseling.","C":"The hospital must perform the screening examination, but it may condition stabilizing treatment on proof of insurance once an emergency condition is identified.","D":"The hospital may transfer the client before screening or stabilization whenever insurance is absent, provided another emergency department is geographically nearby."}}
questions.rationale: EMTALA requires a Medicare-participating hospital with a dedicated emergency department to provide an appropriate medical screening examination when an individual comes seeking examination or treatment for a possible emergency medical condition. If an emergency medical condition exists, the hospital must provide stabilizing treatment within its capability or an appropriate transfer; examination or treatment may not be delayed to inquire about payment method or insurance status.
questions.source_name: eCFR — 42 CFR §489.24, Special responsibilities of Medicare hospitals in emergency cases
questions.source_detail: 42 CFR §489.24(a), (c), and (d): appropriate medical screening examination; no delay in examination/treatment to inquire about payment; stabilizing treatment or appropriate transfer when an emergency medical condition exists. Current eCFR reviewed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: Three days after major trauma, a client develops acute hypoxemic respiratory failure with new bilateral lung opacities that are not primarily explained by cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The findings most strongly indicate isolated chronic obstructive pulmonary disease because bilateral new opacities are not part of an acute inflammatory lung-injury pattern.","B":"The findings are compatible with acute respiratory distress syndrome when required oxygenation and respiratory-support criteria are also satisfied in the clinical setting.","C":"The findings establish cardiogenic pulmonary edema because bilateral opacities in acute respiratory failure are presumed hydrostatic regardless of the clinical context.","D":"The findings exclude acute respiratory distress syndrome because trauma is not recognized as a precipitating risk factor in the current global ARDS framework."}}
questions.rationale: The current Global Definition describes ARDS as acute hypoxemic respiratory failure from inflammatory lung injury after a predisposing risk factor such as trauma, with bilateral opacities and edema not primarily explained by cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Formal classification also depends on oxygenation and respiratory-support criteria; bilateral opacities alone are insufficient.
questions.source_name: Global ARDS Definition Consensus — A New Global Definition of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
questions.source_detail: Matthay et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2024;209(1):37-47. DOI 10.1164/rccm.202303-0558WS. Consensus definition includes acute hypoxemia, bilateral opacities, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, predisposing risk factors including trauma, and oxygenation/support criteria. Reviewed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client with a T4 spinal cord injury suddenly develops a pounding headache, facial flushing, profuse sweating above the lesion, and blood pressure 210/120 mm Hg. Which nursing action is the priority?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Place the client flat and elevate the legs because the primary problem is loss of vascular tone with severe hypotension from the high spinal cord injury.","B":"Administer routine analgesia and reassess in one hour because headache and sweating are expected chronic manifestations after an injury above T6.","C":"Encourage the client to bear down and increase abdominal pressure because autonomic dysreflexia is usually relieved by increasing stimulation below the lesion.","D":"Sit the client upright, rapidly assess for triggers such as bladder or bowel distention, monitor blood pressure closely, and escalate emergency management."}}
questions.rationale: The presentation is classic for autonomic dysreflexia, a potentially life-threatening hypertensive emergency in people with spinal cord injury, commonly at or above T6. Immediate management includes upright positioning, frequent blood-pressure monitoring, and rapid identification and removal of triggers, especially bladder or bowel problems.
questions.source_name: Paralyzed Veterans of America / Consortium for Spinal Cord Medicine — Evaluation and Management of Autonomic Dysreflexia and Other Autonomic Dysfunctions
questions.source_detail: Current PVA Consortium CPG listing reviewed 2026-08-14. Guideline section on acute autonomic dysreflexia supports immediately sitting the individual upright, frequent blood-pressure monitoring, and prompt search/removal of provoking stimuli, especially urinary or bowel triggers.

questions.stem: A stable postoperative client has hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL and no chest pain, dyspnea, active bleeding, orthostatic symptoms, or hemodynamic instability. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The hemoglobin is low, but transfusion decisions should consider the full clinical context and symptoms rather than treating 9.2 g/dL as an automatic transfusion trigger.","B":"A hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL requires immediate red-cell transfusion in every postoperative adult regardless of symptoms, comorbidities, stability, or evidence of active bleeding.","C":"The result is normal for an adult after surgery, so no trend, bleeding assessment, or clinical correlation is needed unless hemoglobin falls below 5 g/dL.","D":"The value proves active internal hemorrhage because postoperative anemia cannot result from perioperative blood loss, hemodilution, or preexisting anemia."}}
questions.rationale: The 2023 AABB international guideline recommends a restrictive red-cell transfusion strategy for most hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults, generally considering transfusion below 7 g/dL, while emphasizing symptoms and the overall clinical context. A hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL in this stable asymptomatic client is not a universal automatic transfusion indication.
questions.source_name: AABB International Panel — Red Blood Cell Transfusion: 2023 AABB International Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Carson et al., JAMA. 2023;330(19):1892-1902. DOI 10.1001/jama.2023.12914. Recommendation 1: restrictive strategy for hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults, generally considering transfusion when hemoglobin is <7 g/dL; clinical context and symptoms should inform decisions. Reviewed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client has a heavily exudative sacral wound with repeated strike-through drainage and early periwound maceration. Which dressing strategy best addresses the immediate wound-management problem?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Select an absorptive dressing appropriate for heavy exudate and protect the periwound skin while reassessing drainage and wound characteristics.","B":"Use a transparent film as the primary dressing because occlusion is preferred even when drainage repeatedly saturates the existing dressing.","C":"Leave the wound uncovered so drainage can evaporate, relying on linen changes rather than an absorptive dressing to control the excess moisture.","D":"Continue dry gauze on a fixed schedule regardless of saturation because changing the dressing based on exudate unnecessarily disrupts wound healing."}}
questions.rationale: Heavy exudate requires a dressing strategy that controls excess moisture and protects the surrounding skin from maceration. WOCN's wound-management framework identifies excessive fluid as a cause of wound-edge maceration and supports moisture-balancing or fluid-removal approaches selected to match the wound's characteristics.
questions.source_name: WOCN — Wound Management VLU / TIME Framework
questions.source_detail: WOCN VLU wound-management content, adapted from Ermer-Seltun & Rolstad (2022), General Principles of Topical Therapy in WOCN Core Curriculum: Wound Management, 2nd ed.: excessive fluid causes wound-margin maceration and requires moisture-balancing/fluid-removal methods. Reviewed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: An older adult with delirium from a urinary infection repeatedly tries to climb out of bed. Which nursing action is most appropriate before considering a physical restraint?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Administer a sedating medication primarily to keep the client in bed, because chemical restraint is less restrictive than a physical device.","B":"Raise all side rails and leave the client alone in a dark room so environmental stimulation cannot contribute to further attempts to get up.","C":"Apply a waist restraint while the family is present, then evaluate reversible causes after the immediate fall risk has been controlled.","D":"Increase observation, address reversible causes, use environmental safety measures, and try less-restrictive interventions before restraint."}}
questions.rationale: Federal hospital patient-rights regulations require restraint to be used only when less-restrictive interventions have been determined ineffective and require the least restrictive intervention that will effectively protect the patient or others. In a delirious client, observation, treatment of reversible causes, and environmental safety measures should therefore be attempted before restraint when clinically feasible.
questions.source_detail: 42 CFR §482.13(e)(2)-(3): restraint/seclusion may be used only when less restrictive interventions have been determined ineffective and must be the least restrictive intervention that will be effective to protect the patient, staff, or others. Current eCFR reviewed 2026-08-14.
